note: Faithful rendering of the end of MMK ch. 23 and the opening objection verses of ch. 24 with their commentary; verse and prose correctly separated.

errors.english: because you yourself accept that at the time of arising
errors.why: The Tibetan says that on the opponent's own assertion (connection with impermanence at arising) it has just been shown that the entity does not exist even for a moment; the opponent does not himself accept that conclusion.

note: A sound rendering of a dense argument on arising and destruction; one point where the author's conclusion is put in the opponent's mouth.

errors.english: Because there is little to discuss later, in order to explain "unmistaken" first
errors.why: The Tibetan says that although 'unmistaken' is stated later in the definition, it is explained first because there is little to say about it.

fix.find: Because there is little to discuss later, in order to explain "unmistaken" first
fix.replace: Although it is stated later [in the definition], because there is little to say about it, in order to explain "unmistaken" first

errors.english: If it is asked, "Is it not so that one will not mistakenly regard it as valid cognition?"
errors.why: The objector gives a purpose: '[it is said] so that one does not mistake it for valid cognition'; it is not a question.

note: Good on the timira/firebrand examples and the abhrānta argument; the reason for explaining 'unmistaken' first is misread.

errors.english: Even if there is a gathering [note: an assembly of conditions]
errors.why: In this argument against the Nyāya self, འདུ་བ is samavāya, inherence (cognition inheres in the self), not an assembly of conditions.

fix.find: Even if there is a gathering [note: an assembly of conditions]
fix.replace: Even though [cognition] inheres [in it] [note: samavāya, inherence]

errors.english: because there is no transformation, there is no contradiction in this being a permanent entity even regarding the transformation of the nature of cognition.
errors.why: This sentence is part of the opponent's thought closed by སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པ་ལ, but the English presents it as the commentator's own statement before 'One might think'.

errors.english: Because if that were the case, it would change.
errors.why: The root says that memory changes when that (experience and its traces) changes, as the gloss immediately explains; it is not a counterfactual.

note: The thread of the anti-ātman argument is broadly followed, but the opponent's view is not separated from the reply and the key term samavāya is lost.

errors.english: Then, after requesting the Blessed One and receiving his command, the monk [note: Anathapindika] went to the city of Shravasti [note: original: mnyan yod] together with Shariputra.
errors.why: The monk is Śāriputra, assigned by the Buddha's command (Skt. tad-ādiṣṭena śāriputreṇa bhikṣuṇā); Anāthapiṇḍika is a householder, not a monk.

fix.find: Then, after requesting the Blessed One and receiving his command, the monk [note: Anathapindika] went to the city of Shravasti [note: original: mnyan yod] together with Shariputra.
fix.replace: Then, having made his request to the Blessed One, he went to the city of Shravasti [note: original: mnyan yod] together with the monk Shariputra, appointed by the Blessed One's command.

note: A good rendering of the Tibetan verses of the Jetavana story (the interleaved Sanskrit is correctly left as parallel); one misidentified monk.

errors.english: Others qualify the reason by saying that it acts as the prover of the probandum through the prior statement.
errors.why: Others qualify the former (similarity/dissimilarity) with 'proving the probandum'; 'through the prior statement' misreads སྔ་མས.

note: The critique of the Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika definitions of the reason is followed adequately; a few sentences are loose but the argument survives.

errors.english: great compassion—which desires to be free from previous suffering—
errors.why: སྔར་གྱི refers to the great compassion discussed earlier, which wishes beings to be free from suffering, not 'previous suffering'.

note: Clear and accurate account of cittotpāda and the eight abhisamayas; one misattached qualifier.

errors.english: in uncertain things such as (prameya) objects of cognition and so forth
errors.why: མ་ངེས་པ here is the inconclusive (anaikāntika) reason and གཞལ་བྱ་ཉིད is the reason 'being knowable' (prameyatva), the classic inconclusive reason.

fix.find: in uncertain things such as (prameya) objects of cognition and so forth
fix.replace: in inconclusive reasons such as 'being knowable' (prameyatva) and so forth

errors.english: because it is not connected with the sound [note: the verbal designation or label]
errors.why: Sound is the subject of the inference ('sound is permanent/impermanent because visible'); visibility does not occur in sound, so it is unestablished, not doubtful.

fix.find: because it is not connected with the sound [note: the verbal designation or label]
fix.replace: because it is not connected with sound [note: sound, the subject of the inference, is not visible]

errors.english: that which contradicts the reason becomes
errors.why: The Tibetan pairs the valid reason and the contradictory reason, which, when presence and absence are certain, become respectively the proponent's proof and the opponent's refutation.

fix.find: that which contradicts the reason becomes
fix.replace: the reason and the contradictory reason become

errors.english: Stating such a form is the refutation of the opponent.
errors.why: The statement of such doubt is the respondent's (prativādin's) refutation, i.e. a refutation made by the opponent, not of him.

errors.english: would the (sadhya) the object to be proven be a refutation of an inverted object
errors.why: The question is whether what the refuter must prove is an inverted object or an inverted certainty.

note: The dialectic on unestablished and inconclusive reasons is hard to follow because the technical reasons (prameyatva, cākṣuṣatva) and the subject 'sound' are not recognised.

errors.english: To show that there is not no distinction between self and other
errors.why: The Tibetan says there is no distinction between self and other; the double negative reverses it.

fix.find: To show that there is not no distinction between self and other
fix.replace: To show that there is no distinction between self and other

errors.english: rather, if one asks what it is, it is not an inference
errors.why: This is an opponent's claim ('is it not inference?') to which the root 'but if the mind is known through the object' replies; the English makes it the author's denial.

errors.english: if memory is an experience [note: Tibetan: ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བ་, Sanskrit: anubhava], then it is the direct perception
errors.why: It is an opponent's claim that if there is memory of the experience, the experiencing perception is known, answered by the root 'when...'; also 'memory of experience', not 'memory is an experience'.

note: A lemma-by-lemma commentary whose objection/reply markers (ཟེར་བ་ལ) are repeatedly flattened, plus one reversed sentence.
Accurate rendering of the argument that sense perception does not take universals and particulars as its object, with the opponent's view and reply correctly separated.
